public_rationale: Both parts held in 2025. On hype: Sam Altman opened the year saying agents might 'join the workforce', and Gartner said most agent projects were 'mostly driven by hype'. On reliability: CMU's TheAgentCompany benchmark found the best agent finished only 30% of realistic workplace tasks. Gartner judged that current models lack the maturity to achieve complex goals on their own. In October, Andrej Karpathy said such agents 'just don't work'. The main counterpoint is coding agents, which worked well by some practitioners' accounts. The verdict treats coding as the kind of specialised use Marcus's carve-out allows.
limitations: The result partly depends on reading coding agents as a 'narrow use case'. A reader who treats coding as broad could call this mixed.
'Endlessly hyped' and 'far from reliable' set no thresholds.

our_interpretation: The claim has two parts. (1) Hype: prominent industry figures and vendors heavily promote AI agents during 2025. (2) Reliability: on general multi-step tasks, agents complete well under most tasks or are judged unreliable by credible evaluators. Success in some narrow areas is allowed by his carve-out.
Whether coding agents count as a 'very narrow use case' is open. Here they are treated as a specialised domain, not as general-purpose agents.

criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible 2025 evidence that agents worked reliably across broad, varied real-world tasks, for example high completion rates on realistic workplace benchmarks, or wide dependable deployment beyond narrow niches. Alternatively, evidence that agents were not heavily hyped.
